moduleTitle: Lesson 1 - Mobile Engine 3.0 & the Tricentis Mobile Agent
learningObjectives: Describe what the Tricentis Mobile Agent (TMA) does and what manual toolchain work it removes.
Explain how Mobile Engine 3.0 relates to Appium under the hood without exposing that complexity to the tester.
List the platforms and app types Mobile Engine 3.0 supports.
Distinguish the roles of TMA (device/session management) from Mobile Engine 3.0 (steering and TestCase execution).

elements.description: Automating a mobile app with raw Appium normally means: installing Appium and its Node.js dependencies, installing Java, wiring up platform-specific drivers (UiAutomator2 for Android, XCUITest for iOS), managing environment variables and PATH entries, and writing test scripts in a supported language. None of that is Tosca-specific — it is the general cost of mobile test automation before you write a single test.

elements.term: TMA removes the toolchain, not the underlying engine
elements.description: The Tricentis Mobile Agent (TMA) provides simplified setup and configuration of iOS and Android devices. You do not install Appium, Java components, or configure environment variables yourself — TMA bundles and manages that layer. Underneath, Mobile Engine 3.0 still drives sessions the same way Appium-based tools do (UiAutomator2 on Android, XCUITest on iOS); TMA is what hides that machinery behind a device list and a Start/Stop toggle.

elements.text: Knowing that Appium sits underneath is useful for troubleshooting — error messages from a failed session sometimes surface raw Appium/driver text — but day-to-day authoring never requires touching Appium directly.

bulletPoints: No manual Appium, Java, or environment-variable setup — TMA owns that layer.
Underneath: UiAutomator2 for Android, XCUITest for iOS — visible mainly in error messages, not in daily use.

elements.description: A standalone application, installed separately from Tosca Commander, that manages device connectivity: it lists connected/available devices, emulators, and simulators, reports their status (Ready, Busy, Offline), starts and stops automation sessions, and exposes a REST API that both the TMA console and Tosca itself talk to.

The Engine inside Tosca that steers mobile applications through a TMA session. Once Modules exist, the TestCase-building workflow is the familiar Tosca one — Modules, TestSteps, TestStepValues, ActionModes — identical in shape to XBrowser or any other Engine. The mobile-specific work lives in the connection and scanning setup, not in how TestCases are structured.

elements.title: Division of responsibility
items: TMA: device discovery, session lifecycle, install/uninstall of apps under test, the REST API Tosca connects through.
Mobile Engine 3.0: control identification during Mobile Scan, and steering (click, swipe, type, verify) during TestCase execution.
Tosca Commander: where Modules and TestCases are authored, exactly as with any other Engine.

bulletPoints: TMA = the device/session layer. Mobile Engine 3.0 = the steering layer. Tosca Commander = where you build and run TestCases.

elements.title: What Mobile Engine 3.0 automates
items: Android — physical devices (via USB) and emulators created through Android Studio.
iOS — physical devices and the iOS Simulator, both requiring a Mac running TMA (Xcode dependency).
Native apps — built specifically for the platform, e.g. a compiled Android/iOS app.
Hybrid apps — a native shell hosting embedded web views, common in cross-platform frameworks.
Mobile web — a website opened in the device's own browser, scanned in its device context.

elements.text: All three app types (native, hybrid, mobile web) are reached through the same Mobile Scan and the same Mobile Modules — the difference is in what gets captured during scanning, covered in the Mobile Scan lesson.

bulletPoints: Two platforms (Android, iOS) × three app types (native, hybrid, web) — one engine, one scan, one Module workflow.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Local vs Remote — a first look

elements.description: TMA runs on the same machine as Tosca Commander, connected to a device via USB or to a simulator/emulator on that same machine. This is the simplest topology and the one most learners start with.

TMA runs on a different machine than Tosca Commander — for example a Mac running TMA for iOS work, connected to over the network from a Windows machine running Tosca Commander. Remote is also how shared device farms and CI environments are typically wired.

elements.text: This is only an introduction — the full connection mechanics (TCPs, the TMAServer trailing-slash requirement, the --rest-address startup flag) are covered in depth in the Connecting Tosca to TMA lesson.

bulletPoints: Local = TMA and Tosca Commander on the same machine. Remote = TMA on a different machine, reached over the network.
The choice is a topology/configuration decision — the TestCases themselves do not change.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming Appium must be installed and configured manually
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Setting up Appium, Java components, and environment variables before starting mobile automation in Tosca.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: TMA exists precisely to remove that work — it provides simplified setup and configuration of iOS and Android devices without requiring manual Appium, Java, or environment-variable configuration.

examPitfalls.title: Treating TMA and Mobile Engine 3.0 as the same thing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Referring to 'TMA' when describing how a TestCase steers a control, or to 'Mobile Engine' when describing device connectivity.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: TMA manages devices and sessions; Mobile Engine 3.0 does the scanning and steering inside Tosca. Keep the two separate when troubleshooting — a device-list problem is a TMA problem, a control-identification problem is a Mobile Engine problem.

examPitfalls.title: Expecting iOS automation to work the same way on Windows as Android
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Trying to run TMA for iOS directly on a Windows machine.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: iOS automation depends on Xcode-based tooling (XCUITest), which only exists on macOS. iOS work always needs a Mac somewhere in the topology, whether Tosca Commander itself runs there or connects to it as a Remote (TMA) machine.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the primary job of the Tricentis Mobile Agent (TMA)?

options.text: Authoring TestCases and Modules.
Managing device connectivity, session lifecycle, and exposing a REST API — removing the need to manually configure Appium, Java, and environment variables.
Rendering the mobile app's UI inside Tosca Commander.
Replacing the Mobile Scan entirely.

practiceQuiz.hint: TMA is the setup/connectivity layer, not the authoring layer.
practiceQuiz.rationale: TMA provides simplified setup and configuration of iOS and Android devices, manages sessions, and exposes a REST API — so you never manually install Appium, Java components, or configure environment variables. Authoring TestCases happens in Tosca Commander via Mobile Engine 3.0.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which app types can Mobile Engine 3.0 automate through the Mobile Scan? (three correct answers)

options.text: Native apps
Hybrid apps (native shell with embedded web views)
Mobile web (device browser)
Desktop-only Windows applications

practiceQuiz.hint: Two platforms, three kinds of app — desktop apps belong to a different Engine (WinX/UIA).
practiceQuiz.rationale: Mobile Engine 3.0 covers native, hybrid, and mobile web apps through the same Mobile Scan. Desktop Windows applications are automated through the WinX/UIA Engine, not Mobile Engine 3.0.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which underlying technology does Mobile Engine 3.0 rely on for iOS device automation?

options.text: UiAutomator2
XCUITest
Selenium WebDriver
A proprietary Tricentis-only protocol with no Appium relationship

practiceQuiz.hint: It is Xcode-based, which is why iOS automation needs a Mac.
practiceQuiz.rationale: iOS automation runs on XCUITest (Android uses UiAutomator2), both Appium-standard drivers that TMA manages behind the scenes. XCUITest's Xcode dependency is exactly why iOS automation requires a Mac somewhere in the topology.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A tester says: 'The control isn't being recognised correctly during the Mobile Scan.' Which component is most likely responsible?

options.text: TMA, since it owns device connectivity.
Mobile Engine 3.0, since it performs control identification and steering.
Tosca Commander's licensing module.
The device's mobile network carrier.

practiceQuiz.hint: Separate 'can Tosca see the device' problems from 'can Tosca recognise this control' problems.
practiceQuiz.rationale: TMA handles whether a device is discoverable and session-ready. Once a session exists, control identification and steering during scanning and execution are Mobile Engine 3.0's job — that is where a recognition problem belongs.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What benefit does the Tricentis Mobile Agent (TMA) provide for mobile app testing?

options.text: Enhanced manual testing capabilities
Faster testing without setup hassles for the latest devices
Support for testing only hybrid apps
Integration with cloud platforms for device management

practiceQuiz.hint: Think about what TMA removes from the traditional mobile automation toolchain.
practiceQuiz.rationale: TMA's core benefit is removing manual toolchain setup — Appium, Java components, environment variables, drivers — so testing against current devices can start right away. It doesn't enhance manual testing, and it isn't limited to hybrid apps; cloud device-farm integration exists through specific Modules but isn't TMA's defining benefit.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which of the following statements about Tricentis Tosca Mobile is false?

options.text: Enables seamless testing on public and private clouds
Eliminates configuration challenges for testing across Windows and Mac
Depends on technical complexities for using Appium
Supports compatibility testing for various OS, browsers, and devices

practiceQuiz.hint: One option directly contradicts what TMA exists to remove.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Tosca Mobile is built specifically so testers do not need to deal with Appium's technical complexity — TMA hides that layer entirely. 'Depends on technical complexities for using Appium' is therefore the false statement; the other three describe genuine capabilities.

quickRecap.value: Device discovery, session lifecycle, REST API — removes manual Appium/Java/environment-variable setup.
Control identification (scanning) and steering (execution) inside Tosca, using the familiar Module/TestCase workflow.
UiAutomator2 (Android), XCUITest (iOS) — both Appium-standard, both hidden behind TMA in normal use.
Android (device or Android Studio emulator) and iOS (device or Simulator, Mac required).
Native, hybrid, and mobile web — one Mobile Scan handles all three.
Local = TMA + Tosca on the same machine. Remote = TMA on a different machine, reached over the network. Full mechanics in the Connecting Tosca to TMA lesson.
